items.title: Dissociation between muscle activation, spinal joint load, and subjective perception in passive back support exoskeleton use
items.license: CC BY 4.0 (verified on article pages; occasional CC0)
items.abstract: by Hyeonhee Jung, Jangwhan Ahn, Eunsik Choi, Jeongin Moon, Kyoungchul Kong, Jooeun Ahn One important purpose of back support exoskeletons (BSEs) is to reduce the stress to the lumbar spine and alleviate the low back pain. However, most previous studies introducing BSEs have argued for their effectiveness based only on easily measurable physiological outcomes such as muscle activation. Motivated by this gap, we examined whether the muscle activation of the back muscle during load handling with a passive BSE can faithfully reflect the estimated L5–S1 joint reaction forces and subjective perceptions. Experiments involving 12 healthy young adults revealed that the BSE significantly reduced average thoracic erector spinae muscle activation during both lifting and lowering the load, and lumbar erector spinae muscle activation during lowering. The BSE also reduced integrated thoracic erector spinae muscle activation during lowering. L5–S1 joint reaction forces were also significantly reduced by the BSE (p < 0.001). Participants reported a lower rate of perceived exertion (p < 0.05). However, the lack of associations among all metrics suggests that inferring one measure from another remains limited when evaluating the efficacy of a BSE.

items.title: Mapping the topographic organization of the human zona incerta using diffusion MRI
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: The zona incerta (ZI) is a deep brain region originally described by Auguste Forel as an ‘immensely confusing area about which nothing can be said’. Despite the elusive nature of this structure, mounting evidence supports the role of the ZI and surrounding regions across a diverse range of brain functions and as a candidate target for neuromodulatory therapies. Using in vivo diffusion magnetic resonance imaging and data-driven connectivity, we identify a topographic organization between the ZI and neocortex. Specifically, our methods identify a rostral–caudal gradient predominantly connecting the frontopolar and ventral prefrontal cortices with the rostral ZI, and the primary sensorimotor cortices with the caudal ZI. Moreover, we demonstrate how clustering and gradient approaches build complementary evidence including facilitating the mapping of a central region of the ZI, connected with the dorsal prefrontal cortex. These results were shown to be replicable across multiple datasets and at the individual subject level, building evidence for the important role of the ZI in mediating frontal lobe-associated tasks, ranging from motor to cognitive to emotional control. items.title: Mycobacterium tuberculosis suppresses protective Th17 responses during infection
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) causes more deaths annually than any other pathogen, yet an effective vaccine remains elusive. IFN-γ-producing Th1 CD4+ T cells are necessary but insufficient for protection against infection. items.title: Complementary stable and dynamic prelimbic ensembles encode learned threat value underlying generalization and discrimination
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: Adaptive behavior requires assigning emotional value to sensory cues and generalizing to similar stimuli. The prelimbic cortex (PL) is critical for threat expression and discrimination, yet its neuronal ensembles undergo substantial turnover over time. How stable population codes emerge despite this reorganization remains unknown. Using longitudinal calcium imaging in freely moving mice, we tracked PL activity for 30 days during auditory discriminative fear learning and retrieval. Despite substantial ensemble turnover, stable graded representations persisted in PL populations. A generalized linear model showed that the tone threat value explained graded activity better than freezing, indicating that PL primarily encodes stimulus significance. Population similarity across stimulus presentations was highest for shock-associated and highly generalized tones, suggesting a stable population code underlying threat generalization. Stable neurons preserved graded gradients across sessions, whereas learning modulated the rate of dynamic frequency-selective neurons. Together, these populations enabled stable threat-value coding despite ongoing ensemble reorganization.

items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: Planning is critical for adaptive behaviour in a changing world, because it lets us anticipate the future and adjust our actions accordingly. While prefrontal cortex is crucial for this process, it remains unknown how planning is implemented in neural circuits. Prefrontal representations were recently discovered in simpler sequence memory tasks, where different populations of neurons represent different future time points. We demonstrate that combining such representations with the ubiquitous principle of neural attractor dynamics allows circuits to solve much richer problems, including planning. This is achieved by embedding the environment structure directly in synaptic connections to implement an attractor network that infers desirable futures. The resulting ‘spacetime attractor’ excels at planning in challenging tasks known to depend on the prefrontal cortex. items.title: Host–virus interactions dominate fitness and conceal additive genetic variation
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: by Aleksei Belyi, Yiyang Du, Alastair J. Wilson, Ben Longdon, Francis M. Jiggins Host–parasite coevolution is expected to generate strong selection for resistance and infectivity that has the potential to erode genetic variation. Despite this, natural populations often retain extensive genetic variation in these traits. Genotype-by-genotype interactions on fitness can generate negative frequency-dependent selection, which helps maintain this variation by preventing any host or pathogen genotype from retaining a permanent advantage. Because these interactions place genetic variance in the interaction term rather than in additive differences among hosts or pathogens, that variance is masked from directional selection and can remain ‘cryptic’. Here we combine coevolutionary modelling with large‑scale experimental infection assays to quantify how host-pathogen interactions structure fitness variance in a vertically transmitted virus system, Drosophila melanogaster and sigma virus. Simulations show that coevolution typically erodes additive genetic variance in host and pathogen fitness, concentrating variance in host-virus interaction terms. Consistent with these predictions, experiments spanning 90 host-virus genotype combinations reveal that transmission, viral load, and virulence are overwhelmingly governed by host-virus genetic interactions rather than host or virus main effects

items.title: A cortical semantic map integrates fractions and integers in the human brain
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: by Daniela Valério, Samuel Debray, Alireza Karami, Maxime Cauté, Nicolás Gravel, Stanislas Dehaene How does the human brain represent the meaning of abstract symbols? Some theories postulate the existence of semantic spaces where concepts occupy positions that reflect their conceptual relationships. In the number domain, psychological evidence suggests that integers are represented along a mental number line which, with education, integrates higher-level number concepts such as fractions. To test this hypothesis, we recorded whole-brain 7T fMRI responses to integer and fraction symbols during an active magnitude comparison task designed to engage magnitude processing. Consistent with predictions, we found both behavioral and neural numerical distance effects. Activation vectors in intraparietal, inferior temporal, prefrontal, hippocampal, and parahippocampal cortices formed a two-dimensional semantic space organized by numerical magnitude and domain (fractions versus integers). Gaussian fits revealed a topographic map of numerical preferences in the anterior inferior parietal cortex, common to both domains. Our results suggest that, when educated adults engage in an explicit magnitude comparison task, their brain can construct an ordered representation that integrates fractions and integers, with a topographic organization in the anterior IPS/IPL.

items.title: Mid-zone hepatocytes trade proliferation for survival via Atf4-Chop axis in early acute liver injury
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: Hepatocytes undergo extensive proliferation to facilitate liver repair after injury, yet early adaptive changes prior to proliferation remain unclear. Using a mouse model of acetaminophen (APAP)-induced liver injury, we show that hepatocytes undergo transient proliferation suppression that is most pronounced in mid-zone hepatocytes, consistent with zonal APAP metabolism. Although spatial transcriptomics (ST) alone could not independently confirm zonal proliferative restraint, ST analysis identified a unique mid-zone stress-response program centered on the Atf4-Chop axis. By integrating Cut&Run with immunohistochemistry and functional studies, we found that the Atf4-Chop axis suppresses proliferation via the cell-cycle inhibitor Btg2. Together, our findings support a model in which mid-zone hepatocytes transiently prioritize stress adaptation over proliferation, thereby preserving regenerative capacity for subsequent liver repair.

items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: Nutrient resorption is a key plant strategy for nutrient conservation, yet whether it responds plastically to non-nutrient stressors such as salinity remains unresolved. items.title: Benchmarking miRNA Target Prediction Methods
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: Background: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) regulate gene expression by binding to target mRNAs. Although many tools predict miRNA-target interactions, predictions show limited concordance, and benchmarks relying on curated databases may be biased by overlap with tool-development data. Methods: We benchmarked seven tools (TargetScan, miRDB, miRmap, DIANA-microT, RNA22, miRWalk, and mirDIP) across approximately 59.7 million candidate miRNA-mRNA pairs. Each pair received an evidence-graded reference score (0-3) combining validated interactions from miRTarBase and TarBase with expression-derived evidence from paired miRNA-seq and mRNA-seq data in an induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) cohort of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome and control lines. Performance was evaluated using Type I error, statistical power, and false discovery proportion (FDP). Robustness was assessed by increasing reference-score stringency (truth signal) and including progressively lower-confidence predictions (model signal). Optimal cutoffs maximized Youden's J statistic. Results: Rankings were largely consistent across settings. TargetScan and miRDB maintained Type I error rates below 0.05, with TargetScan showing the lowest FDP, but both had limited power. mirDIP achieved the highest power at the cost of the highest Type I error rate. At optimal cutoffs, mirDIP best balanced sensitivity and specificity (Youden's J = 0.566), followed by DIANA-microT (J = 0.481); miRWalk and RNA22 had FDPs near the random-prediction baseline. No tool was optimal across all metrics; tool and cutoff selection should reflect whether sensitivity or specificity is prioritized."""

items.title: MechGate: combining mechanism-derived measures of permeation and efflux to screen small molecule drugs targeting Escherichia coli
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: Most antibiotic molecules must cross the cell membrane and escape efflux pumps before hitting their targets. For de novo antibiotic design, very few of the in-silico-generated drug molecules can successfully pass these two steps. Existing evaluations of generated molecules do not separate these steps. Therefore, we introduce MechGate, a mechanism-resolved screening tool evaluating small drug molecules against E. coli, measuring permeation, efflux and antibacterial activity. After SMILES input, five measures are reported side by side: two for permeation via porins, one for permeation via the phospholipid membrane, one for efflux and one for activity. Each measure is read on its own, so a molecule that fails can be traced to the step that stops it. All features are taken from papers that state their mechanism rather than selected by importance ranking. On an external set of marketed antibacterials the measures give a precision of 0.789 to 0.873 against baselines near 0.44, and combining them the way the mechanism predicts raises precision to 0.92. We also find that the four public source libraries are separable from one another using physicochemical features alone; every measure here therefore draws both classes from a single library. All code is open-source and requires no commercial software.

items.title: Agent-guided epitope excision enables economical de novo binder design
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: De novo protein design campaigns remain bottlenecked by the inference compute time required to generate and rank candidates, limiting wider functional exploration. Here, we introduce and evaluate an epitope excision approach that truncates targets to local interface windows to accelerate both backbone diffusion and structure prediction. Across 15 targets and 3,666 designs, excised windows closely reproduced full-target binding interfaces (median CαRMSD of 0.37 Å) and made it practical to design binders against the 719-residue extracellular domain of fibroblast activation protein alpha (FAP) by cutting RFdiffusion and AlphaFold3 GPU time by ~ 88% in one of the epitopes. Pairing this workflow with an agentic optimization loop allowed the system to autonomously identify catalytic-site targeting strategies. Under a fixed compute budget, a human-in-the-loop (HITL) workflow raised the computational hit rate from 5.06% to 9.33% while further cutting GPU hours by ~ 42%. We also found that omitting target multiple sequence alignments during refolding roughly substantially increased the apparent yield. Wet-lab validation with yeast display identified nanomolar binders from the generated designs with the HITL and the fully autonomous agent (human-out-of-the-loop, HOOTL) arms recovering more enriched designs than the PI-alone baseline. Together, target excision and agent-guided search offer a practical way to scale de novo binder design to large, therapeutically relevant proteins.

items.title: Supercoiling Drives DNA-Protein Co-Condensation
items.license: arXiv API terms; metadata CC0
items.abstract: The co-condensation of DNA and proteins plays an important role in genome compaction, including heterochromatin formation and chromosome segregation. Meanwhile, transcription and replication continuously generate DNA supercoiling, yet how the resulting torsional stress affects co-condensation remains poorly understood. Here, by coupling DNA elasticity to a protein concentration field, we show that supercoiling acts as a topological catalyst for co-condensation through a mutually reinforcing interplay with protein wetting. Specifically, protein wetting facilitates twist-to-writhe conversion, generating highly writhed DNA conformations that in turn promote capillary collapse into a protein-rich droplet. In the absence of supercoiling, DNA remains kinetically trapped in metastable extended states within our model, whereas sufficiently strong supercoiling removes the nucleation barrier and enables spontaneous co-condensation. These results establish topology as a distinct control parameter for biomolecular condensation and provide a mechanical framework for how active genomic processes can dynamically regulate large-scale genome organization.

items.title: Large language models poorly capture how word order shapes representations of sentence meaning in the human brain
items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: Large language models based on the transformer architecture are now capable of producing human-like language. But do they encode and process linguistic meaning in a human-like way? Here, we address this question by analysing 7T fMRI data from 30 participants reading 108 sentences each. These sentences are carefully designed to disentangle sentence structure from word meaning, thereby testing whether transformer representations of sentence meaning resemble those formed by the brain. Using representational similarity analysis, we compared representations from eight transformers and eleven other semantic models to brain activity in language regions of interest. We found that while transformer models match brain representations better than models that completely ignore word order, all transformers poorly match human brain representations of sentences that require sensitivity to structural relations such as semantic roles (who did what to whom). Further, transformers were significantly inferior to models explicitly designed to encode the structural relations between words. Our results provide insight into the nature of sentence representation in the brain, highlighting the critical role of sentence structure. They also cast doubt on the claim that transformers represent sentence meaning similarly to the human brain.

items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: by Susanne Dahle, Gaute T. Einevoll, Torbjørn V. Ness There is an urgent need for better treatment options for many neurological conditions, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, depression, and epilepsy. Transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) is a non-invasive, safe, inexpensive, and promising method that could address some of this unmet need. The therapeutic value of tES has been well demonstrated, but the effect is highly variable. To enable tES to reach its full potential requires a better understanding of how tES modulates neural activity so that tES treatments can be tailored to specific neurological conditions and individual patients. The neural response to tES is, however, highly complex, and the parameter space involved in optimizing tES treatments is daunting. items.license: CC BY 4.0
items.abstract: by Laurel Fogarty, Rebecca B. Hoyle Many human cultural and technological traits have a complex and peculiar structure. They are often characterized by multiple closely interacting parts that can form modules, and change as a result of innovation, collaboration, and social learning. A full understanding of the ways in which such cultural traits evolve requires a model that accounts for the close epistatic interaction of the constituent parts, and for the uniquely cultural processes that act on them. Here, we generalize the concept of ‘adaptive landscapes’, where populations search a landscape for optimal combinations of components. This generalization accounts for epistatic interactions, and includes processes such as modularization, communication, and collaboration, that are not features of genetic systems but may be quite common features of cultural systems.
